Agriculture-Experimental Farms, $1,440,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Probably it would facilitate the work of the committee if I were to give a short explanation of the increase of $40,000 over last year. This has to be utilized for specific purposes. One of these is the extension of the Harrow tobacco farm which was undertaken last summer. This was formerly a small tobacco station, but the work has extended into the growing and breeding of corn, and it was found desirable to add about 200 acres to the farm. The sum of $10,000 will be used for the purpose of getting the farm in shape, plotting it out, making roads through it and doing all the things necessary to carry on experimental work. A similar amount is being expended at Invermere, where a small farm existed, and was organized ten or twelve years ago with the idea of developing it as a fruit farm. The altitude, however, was too great and the temperature too low to be suitable for fruitgrowing purposes. Therefore we are developing that also into a general farm. For this purpose something like 300 acres was transferred from the Soldier Settlement Board. It was some soldier settlement land that had lasped back to the department. This land was transferred to the Experimental Farm branch, and this made the necessary addition to convert the Invermere farm into a regularly constituted farm. This farm is in an irrigation area, and well adapted for potato growing, poultry raising and so on. Some buildings were erected on it last year, but this $10,000 is to develop the farm, complete the fencing and ditching, and provide the general equipment, so that it may be utilized for the purpose intended.
A further $10,000 of this amount is to be used for the establishment of additional illustration stations. We find that we have all kinds of ideas regarding experimental farms. Some people have no use for a little illustration station. They would not be bothered with it in their neighbourhood. They see a post in the ground with a board on it stating it is a Dominion illustration station, and when you speak of these stations they look upon them with disdain. They want a great big farm of 300 acres fully equipped with stock and buildings, and they have no use for these little farms. There is another class of people that have no use

Supply-A griculture

for the regular large experimental farm. They say: They are run by the government and therefore they cannot be much good; the men are paid salaries by the government; they do not work very hard and they are looking for sundown and their salaries. So these people think that such farms are not of much account. They want a small farm, an illustration station. We find, however, that the kind of farm work that is increasing in popularity more than any other is these small illustration stations consisting of forty acres that the government does not buy but merely rents from a resident settler that is of an experimental turn of mind. We enter into a contract with him, renting his property at five dollars an acre, supplying seed and everything else required for working out experiments best adapted to that area. These are particularly popular in the soldier settlement areas. Some of these boys that have taken up farming have been rather unfortunate in their location, sometimes, perhaps, through the fault of nobody in particular. But they are having a hard struggle and are just able to wiggle along. These men appreciate very much any assistance that can be given to them in the way of demonstrating the best method of conducting farming operations in their particular district. I have more especially in mind a number of illustration stations established in Manitoba around Dauphin that have been very beneficial to these soldier settlers who are starting out anew and who are badly involved, without much experience and in need of some assistance from the government. These illustration stations seem to be filling a real need and appealing to a large number of people who like to see work done by what we call a dirt farmer himself, a man on the land that they know, working out these problems without the halo of having a government salary associated with him. That is just an idea that some people have and they derive a great deal of benefit from these little illustration stations On the other hand, others receive greater benefit from the larger experimental farms and would not thank you for the little ones. There is $10,000 for that, $10,000 for the Harrow farm, $10,000 for the tobacco and corn farm, and $10,000 for the extension of the Invermere farm. If we have the money to spare, we have thought of re-establishing a tobacco station at L'As-somption in the county of Montcalm-Terre-bonne. There was a tobacco station there some years ago on rented property, but the land did not prove suitable for growing tobacco. Tobacco growing requires a special character of light soil, and there are in Canada 51
only a few such places, one of them being in the Windsor country in Essex county and two or three places in Quebec which are peculiarly adapted for growing tobacco. We are thinking of devoting $5,000 to the re-establishment of a tobacco farm there if we haye the money for that purpose, and we think we shall have that by exercising a little economy in other directions. The farm was never re-established during the war period and so we are taking it up now. These are the explanations regarding the increases.
With regard to the experimental farm system proper which consists of the Central experimental farm at Ottawa and something like twenty-three branch farms, the Central experimental farm is spoken of as a farm. We think of it as a farm, but it is really a research agricultural bureau with branch activities in different parts of Canada. Not over one-half of the money that is devoted to the Central experimental farm is spent on the farm proper. Out of the moneys expended there over $300,000 are devoted to research work in the various branch farms throughout Canada, but the money is charged up to the Central farm. The sum of $107,000 is devoted to running this farm itself and when you deduct the revenues derived from it, amounting to $65,000, which are returned to the treasury, that leaves a net balance of thirty-two thousand dollars odd against the Central experimental farm. This Central farm has not had its farm areas extended since its organization something like forty years ago. Part of the land has been taken up for an arboretum, part for extensive lawns and borders, shelter beds, orchards and vegetable gardens, so that the farm proper now is reduced to about 235 acres, or about one-half of the original acreage. Therefore, it stands very much in need of extension for fanning purposes.
With regard to branch farms, our policy, since I have had the responsibility of trying to guide the destinies of these institutions, has been not to establish any more branch farms until we had the old twenty-three in better shape. I believe that has been the correct policy. It is not an easy matter to carry it out. The government that preceded us started nine new branch farms in different parts of Canada, a number in the Maritimes and a number in the west. The government that preceded that again started nine branch farms. The government responsible for starting these farms, that led by Sir John A. Macdonald, started five, making in all twenty-three farms. We have stopped establishing new farms until such time that we get the others already estab-

Supply-A griculture

lished in reasonably good shape. That is speaking generally as to the situation. If we come back again to the Central experimental farm, if members of the committee interested in the matter, should so desire, I will give the subdivisions of the work that goes on at the Central farm showing the nature of the research work. Hundreds and thousands of experiments are conducted from year to year, and I shall be glad to give some of the results therefrom, if hon. members so desire. These are the subdivisions: Chemistry, horticulture, cereals, botany, animal husbandry, field husbandry, tobacco, poultry, agristology, bacteriology, illustration stations, extension and publicity, bees, fibre plants. The total amount expended under these various subdivisions I can give, but I had better leave it where it is and let members of the committee ask what they desire as to these particular subdivisions, or any work regarding the branch farms or illustration stations, or any other matters they may desire information about.

Is this the vote under
which the new residence for the superintendent at Fredericton is being built?

No. That comes out of the Public Works vote. There is a vote later on in Public Works for new buildings. Part of the work is, however, being done by the experimental farm regular labour and charged up to the Public Works vote. The work, as I think my hon. friend knows, has been under way for ten years, since the year of the war. Last year we conceived the idea of cleaning up some rough land that was an eyesore from the railway and using the stone from that to build a residence for the superintendent. They had not enough to finish it last year, so we hoped to complete it another year. The same force of men that cleaned the land was used to build the house. There is a way of adjust'ng the accounts

I was wondering why it
was that the minister departed from the well-accepted principle of having work of this kind done by tender, and not cy day labour. The minister did us the honour of visiting us the summer before last, and I understood that he left instructions to have this work done by day labour. I was just wondering why.

That was the reason. It would be pretty hard to get a contractor to go grubbing around in this rough land, hunting up the stones. If he did, I think he would charge up pretty sweetly for it. There is a popular idea too that a contract

is always the cheapest, but that is not necessarily so. In this particular instance better value all round was obtained in the wiay the work was done, having regard to the peculiar material that was used and especially in view of the difficulty we should have experienced in getting the contractor to clean up the land. As it was, the same force that cleaned the land supplied the material for the building, so that they had an interest in getting the best stones they could for the work as well as in cleaning up the place at the same time for the plough.

That is not very convincing, if the minister will allow me to say so. I do not complain particularly but I wondered why there was a departure from the general principle. I have no doubt that the minister could have secured competent contractors in the city of Fredericton to build the house just as it is being put up now, and it would not have been necessary to send out of the immediate community to look for labourers. As far as I am aware, there was not a local stone cutter employed; men were brought from the north shore of New Brunswick to put up the building under the plea that local men were not available. I do not think that this was the fact.

From what vote is the
money to be taken for further research into the rust problem?

That comes under
" Administration of the Destructive Insect and Past Act." With regard to the question raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Hanson), I would point out to him that it takes experience of a special kind to build a wall out of field stone. Some masons will not put a hammer on it at all; they insist on having quarried stone to work on. These being field stones I presume it was found necesary to get outside men who were familiar with this kind of material.

That may be, I do not
know.

I would suggest that
the idea which the public has, that it is better to have tender and contract, is likely the product of the speeches of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) and others in the last parliament.

I was not here;
I think I have read something about it.

The minister is not
guilty; he never had any such heterodox views himself.

I used to have
when I was younger and less familiar with these things. Speaking generally, though, I presume that the contract is the proper method; but it does not always get the best results 'by any means.
The minister means, not the best results politically.

I had no thought
of that this time. Sometimes, however, the intense desire of the contractor to get the contract induces him to bid too low and he either skimps the job or gets into difficulties before he is half through. I am merely defending the day labour system under these peculiar circumstances, and I add, too, that it often proves better even under more favourable conditions. The popular idea of course is that the only right way is the contract way.

There is a line of work I
have been urging the minister to take up in connection with experimental farms and I am glad to see that something is being done in this direction. Yesterday I received a notice indicating that the Civil Service Commission is applying for a horticulturist for the Indian Head experimental farm. I believe that more money devoted to that work would bring good results, for it is research work that would certainly prove beneficial. I have here a clipping showing something of what is being done in the west at the present time. There are some gentlemen in this House who believe that the west is unable to grow fruit; I am sorry that the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) is not present, because I remember his making a reference to this supposition a short time ago. This clipping is short and I shall read it. It has to do with the work of Mr. Tate P. Stevenson of Manitoba, and reads:
RUSSIAN FRUITS THRIVE IN WEST Varieties Introduced by Pioneer Manitoba Horticulturist Are Still Bearing
In front of the old Stevenson home near Morden, Manitoba, stands a Transcendant crab apple tree forty years of age, still bearing fruit in abundance. A little way off is the old apple orchard with its Blushed Calville, Repka Kislaga, Charlamoff, Ostrakoff, Hibernal and other varieties of Russian apple trees, which were loaded with fruit last year. From this orchard Mr. Stevenson harvested one autumn, a few years ago, no less than 300 barrels of apples. Several of the varieties are splendid eating apples, and all of them are first-class cooking fruit. Many varieties of plums have fruited successfully at Pine Grove Nursery, notably the Emerald, Minnesota No. 131, Kaga, Stella, Etopa, and Pembina and several of the newer varieties. The well-known Mammoth plum was developed by the late Mr. Stevenson, being a seedling of the Cheney. Raspberries and strawberries have long been successful fruits at Pine Grove Nursery.
51i	'
Of chief interest to the visitors at Pine Gro/e Nursery was a hedge row of Vladimir cherries. Back in 1891, the late Mr. Stevenson secured a shipment of the then newly introduced hardy Russian cherry trees. Gradually nature thinned them out and cut them down until Mr. Stevenson discarded all except the Vladimir and Shubianca varieties, grown extensively north of Moscow, in Russia, the former being the better in quality. Some of the trees fruited after a few years, there being naturally a great variation in the quality of the fruit. Pits from the best Vladimir fruit were planted, and in due time produced trees which again began to fruit about 10 years ago. Pits from the best of these were again selected and planted. Probably there are 500 to 600 of these cherry trees growing close together in hedge rows six to thirteen feet high, and bearing, in August last, quite abundantly a beautiful bright red cherry. It was rather an inspiring sight to see upwards of 50 people busily engaged eating cherries in a Manitoba orchard. The horticultural experts from eastern Canada pronounced the best of these Vladimir cherries to be quite equal to the best sour cherry produced in Ontario.
To give some idea of what the results might be if a little more attention wer* paid to this department, let me remind the committee of the benefit which the western provinces have derived from the work of Dr. Charles Saunders. Reference was made to this subject before and it will bear emphasis again. Working year after year quietly, and after a considerable period of experimentation,. he was able to produce the marquis wheat, and although it did not involve very much money, the production of that wheat has meant hundreds of millions of dollars to the prairie provinces. One of our leading daily newspapers put it at five hundred million dollars to the world. That may be a large amount but I am not sure that it is over-estimated. Now, the prairies are very bare of fruit, and what was done by Mr. Stevenson, what is being done at Indian Herd in the forestry farm, where they are able to grow an excellent plum, and what a doctor in the town has done, in producing standard apples for a number of years, can be accomplished by departmental activities. At that experimental farm there is a small staff but little attention has been paid to these things. There is an impression in the town nearby where I reside that this work has not been very continuous, nor has it been given any encouragement in past years; in fact, I have heard it rumoured on the streets that on one occasion when there was a fairly good foundation and the trees were ready for grafting, an order was issued that they should be tom up and the place converted into a pasture field. I do not vouch for the truth of that, but it does seem that there has not been sufficient continuous and persistent work along this line; had there been the results would have been better. Certainly, they would
Supply-Agriculture

have been better when you think of what has been done by Mr. Stevenson and others who are known to the department. I was very glad to see that horticulturists were to be engaged, but I have this criticism to make: The salary offered, $1,500, does seem to me to be entirely inadequate for a qualified man to fill such a position in a new country where the foundations for this work are to be laid and three vast prairie provinces to be supplied. I think any man that can be engaged for $1,500 a year is-well, dt does seem to me that he surely cannot have the experience and standing in his profession that he should have. I do not think a salary of $2,500 or $3,000 would be too much; it would be well warranted. However, I am glad that a start has been made. I do hope that a great deal of attention will be paid to this work. The people concerned will appreciate it. It will be easily understood that the individual farmer cannot carry on very much of this work himself; it is too expensive. Fruit trees must be brought from Russia largely. It is well known that we are greatly indebted to that country for a great many of our best hardy varieties of fruit. I will not say that all the money expended on this grant and on experimental farms is wisely spent, but I believe more money might be spent on this department with very good results.

Mr. Chairman, I am very glad to hear my hon. friend from Qu'-Appelle (Mr. Millar) so express himself. We have had representations from Mr. Chip-man and others urging the conversion of some of these farms into strictly fruit farms. That, again, is a question of money, and until people in the west get well established there will not be very much attention devoted to the developing of fruit growing except by a few enthusiasts. As a business proposition, fruit growing at the beginning does not bring very good returns, although of course it affords one a great deal of satisfaction to be able to fill his basket with home grown apples and other fruit. I have had some experience of fruit growing on my own place, and I know it takes a lot of work, work that can ill be spared from other more revenue-producing branches of the farm. Speaking of the late Mr. A. P. Stevenson, I had the pleasure of presenting his family with the Carter medal that was awarded by the Canadian Horticultural Council for having done the most for horticulture, particularly apple growing, in the west. I also had the pleasure of visiting the Morden experimental farm and his old homestead. His orchard was a very interesting place indeed, and you would think you were

in an old established orchard in Ontario to see the large burly limbs well laden with fruit.
Horticulture is a somewhat comprehensive term; to-day it covers vegetables, flowers and fruits. I presume my hon. friend applies the term largely to fruits?
Yes.

Well, it just depends upon how much money we will have available. We have to divert our funds into the avenues that will bring the most practical results to agriculture at this time. It is a matter of opinion as to when we should embark on a more active policy with reference to fruit growing. Fifty years ago this locality was not much better adapted for fruit growing than the district around Indian Head is to-day. I can remember when only an occasional enthusiast grew any considerable number of apples here, but during recent years Mr. W. T. Macoun, Dominion Horticulturist, has evolved, by grafting and by the development of seedlings, eight or ten first class varieties of apples suitable to this climate. They are all excellent for eating, particularly the Melba. Her Excellency Lady Byng is very much interested in this work, and she pronounces them to be very high class apples. Some of these varieties no doubt will be suitable for development in the western country. I will give consideration to my hon. friend's representations -indeed I am doing so now by calling for this assistant horticulturist. With regard to the salary offered, I have always noticed, Mr. Chairman, that the salaries of technical men in agriculture were lower than in any other department. If anyone examines the salaries of technical men, say, in the Mines branch, where engineers are required, and then runs over the salaries of corresponding men in agriculture, he will find the latter are lower for some reason. I am not going to account for it, but they are lower. When young men are starting out in life they choose the vocation which offers the best salaried prospects. If agriculture does not bring as much remuneration as some other profession, naturally they avoid agriculture. Consequently the country develops with comparatively few men available for this class of work, and the salaries are low. I do not want to pass the buck on to the Civil Service Commission, but there is the classification, and I tell you it makes one sweat to get it changed. If my hon. friend, (Mr. Millar) will back me up in insisting that agricultural technical positions should be better paid, probably we will get somewhere. We have

had these positions reclassified, but the Civil Sendee Commission have hundreds of other similar applications, and by the time they' have investigated them probably a year has elapsed, meanwhile the lower salaries prevail and there is no one available for the positions at the lower remuneration. How much money is spent in Ontario outside of the experimental farm in Ottawa?

Last year we added nearly 200 acres to the Harrow farm, and this year we are spending $10,000 to develop it into a general farm, because we find we cannot very well develop a proper tobacco or corn farm without live stock. Then there is the Kapuskasing farm in northern Ontario, doing excellent work where a few years ago was a wilderness. That is one of the few farms I have not visited. I have seen it passing by on the train, and everything looked quite progressive compared with the surrounding country. We have spent about $40,000 at Kapuskasing and $35,000 at Harrow. I think there are eight in this province, at about $300 apiece; then we have $35,000 for Harrow and about $10,000 for Kapuskasing. These, of course, are exclusive of the Ottawa farm. The first agricultural college in Canada was established at Guelph over fifty years ago, so that Ontario has had the benefit of that training and assistance to agriculture, and that may account for the fact that there has not been such a large demand in that province for these small illustration stations.

hear very well, but my deputy has good ears and he told me that what the hon. member wanted was the amount spent in Ontario outside the Central experimental farm. The minister visited the constituency of Nelson in September last. He must have been impressed, not to say surprised, by the agricultural possibilities of that region. Apart altogether from the gardens that he visited-

Does my hon.
friend refer to that portion of the district which is towards its northern extremity?
Yes, I will explain that.

It is pretty hard
to give any estimate of its possibilities after one hurried trip, but I was very much struck with what I saw there in the way of gardens, in the way of grass and in the way of possibilities in many directions which may be considered as sufficient to support a very considerable population. Without entering into railway matters at all-confining myself strictly to agriculture-I found less evidences of frost in the gardens around the Pas than we found around Winnipeg, and up the Swan river. In the newer districts, where the soil is largely what is called muskeg but what is really vegetable matter, the gardens were frozen very badly. But where the soil had been worked for three or four years and the ground solidified and its capacity to contain heat increased, the gardens were in perfect condition. Onions do not grow well there, however; there is too much vegetable matter.
What time of year was that?

The last week in
August. We went on north to mile 81- that is the Herb lake country. The train we were on had something like twenty cars, including the car of settlers' effects. There was no siding on which to spot this car; so it was just set on the track right opposite this man's shack, and the hon. member for Springfield's party I think must have had a time pinch-barring it on and getting their gas car past it. It is quite a trick on that road to spot a car right opposite a man's farm so that another man can get past it. When you get to mile 137, you find there a Hudson's Bay store and other frontier buildings, and evidences of men who in the winter

time devote their attention to trapping, and in the summer to farming operations. At mile 185 there was a gentleman by the name of Cowan. He had a beautiful garden of flowers, and one little apple tree, only about so high, but it had produced its first fruit in the shape of one apple. That was about the last of August. I never inquired how it developed, or whether it wouild suit the particular taste of my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote), but at all events it was an apple. Then os we journeyed further north we came across a cold storage plant at mile 239. It had been filled with sturgeon fish but at the time we got there only one carload was left to ship out. From that on up to mile 332 there was not much evidence of agricuture that I could come to any conclusion about; but the country is not the quagmire or muskeg we hear so much about. It will support a very considerable population engaged in mining, trapping and fishing in the winter, very much the same way of living pursued down in the Maritime provinces, where the people may be engaged in fishing or lumbering at one time of the year, and in farming at another.
I object.

I am not speaking
in disparagement at all. It is a fine thing in a new country to have two or three sources of revenue for the first few years. I cannot remember his name, but the party who was keeping the stopping place at the end of the track was from Cape Breton and knew all the members in this House from Nova Scotia. He and his wife gave us a splendid lodging, and an excellent breakfast next morning at four o'clock when it was time to get back on the train. The whole country up there is capable of considerable agricultural! development, but I do not think you will get much development up there so long as you have better land on the open prairie. Do not mistake me; people are not going to flock in there pell-mell when there is better land easier of access and Closer to the market; but when the Hudson Bay road opens up the farther north country, of course, the closer they will be to their market

I presume that is what my hon. friends across the way wanted to get out of me.

The minister was good
enough when the live stock vote was taken up the other day, to give us permission to speak on live stock in connection with the present vote. The other day during a somewhat long discussion, one very important feature of the live stock business was not

touched on, and that is that while we have expended hundreds of thousands of dollars on exhibitions and the improvement of live stock by the distribution of pure bred sires and in various other ways, at the present time there are still thousands of cattle of very poor quality and in very poor condition being crowded into our markets during the last two or three months of the year, and in that way forcing down the prices in our markets, and so crowding the market with cattle that they can hardly handle the bulk of them. It also tends to lower the market at that time even for the best cattle. In view of this condition and its seriousness to the whole of our agriculture in Canada, I would like to know what the department is doing and has done in the last two or three years towards remedying such a condition, and towards inducing the farmers to finish their cattle in a better way so that they can take them to market and make a better profit on them. The great problem to-day is not so much the quality of the cattle, as the proper feeding of them before sending them to market, and sending them to market at the right time.

Speaking from memory, the latest action we have taken in regard to the improvement of live stock is that we have refused to give indemnity to the owners of grade bulls that are slaughtered for tuberculosis, or for steers of any kind or lump jaw cattle. In order to encourage the farmers to produce a better quality of cattle we have let them know that we are no longer going to indemnify them for animals slaughtered for tuberculosis. That step has just been taken, and that is why I mention it first.
We have also been working in conjunction with the provincial governments where they have had "better live stock" trains, with men going through the country preaching the gospel of better live stock, because after all this is largely an educational matter.
In addition to that we have developed our various branch farms more and more along the line of live stock. I have used the term "live stock breeding depot" in the past, and at such points we are not spending so much time in experimenting with the soil, because in some of the older districts the farmers have a good knowledge of the best cultural methods necessary for their district, but we are giving more attention to live stock and the development of a better quality from grades up by using pure bred males and developing the ordinary cattle along that line. I think that is the cheapest and most practical way for the average man, to take his ordinary female stock, and rather than sell them at a
sacrifice, use a pure bred sire and grade the stock up.
What is being done in the feeding line?

Feeding is a very important matter. There is no virtue in live stock of any kind if you are a bad feeder.
You cannot turn animals out
9	p.m. to take care of themselves and expect to make money out of them. You have to give them not only a maintenance ration, but more, to make them thrive and fatten. We are trying to bring that lesson home, for it is a lesson everyone should know, but like any other missionary work you have to keep pounding it into the people all the time. Some will listen, some will not; but there are always some who believe it.
Then during the last two or three years we have had various stockyard associations at Calgary, Moose Jaw and Winnipeg, working in conjunction with the provincial departments of agriculture and our department in the putting on of three feeder shows. Those owning feeders are encouraged to bring them in there, and those wanting to buy feeders, including Ontario buyers, are encouraged by special freight rates to come out there and buy feeders to take back to Ontario and other eastern provinces. The first show was a remarkable success. Then we put on men to give lectures and addresses on the best way of conducting feeding operations. It seems simple enough but you have to keep on reiterating these things, and we are having remarkable results already. It was really fine at the second feeder show-I was present at the shows at Moose Jaw and Calgary-to see these animals which were nearly all ranch grown animals running on their mothers on the range with that sleekness that you get only from such bred animals. They were in great demand when they arrived at the show, and they ran up to as high as 7 cents, and very many of them 6 cents, for feeders. The Ontario farmers ran them up a little bit because having gone out there so far, and having the advantage of a cheap freight rate they wanted to take back something with them, and they made a good bid; and I have no doubt they will make good returns too. It is just a question of keeping the necessity before them.
In regard to the rubbish to be found in the stockyards, I was quite amazed two years ago, on going to the stockyards at Edmonton, Calgary and Winnipeg, to see the rubbish in those yards. The stock will not pay the freight. They have a very poor quality of

stock, and frequently have no money to buy feed for them, and they have to get rid of them in some way. It is a burden on any man to keep such stock. Where is the responsibility? The branch farms throughout the country, looking at it in a commercial way.

with that experiment as chilled meat last year. We have not the figures here. But a lot of animals fed here were used entirely for that experiment. He buys them at the market price from the farmers, takes them to Swift Current, keeps them in a straw shed, feeds them in the open yard from trench silo with cut com and sunflower and makes good money. I should like to draw the minister's attention to the Hudson Bay railway again. The northern part of the province of Manitoba was delighted and gratified when the minister decided to take his trip up north, and I think they will be equally gratified to learn he has borne his testimony in the House to-night regarding that district:
My purpose in intervening in the discussion to-night is to inquire of the minister whether he has given any consideration to the desirability of instituting an experimental station on some modest lines on some points on the Hudson Bay railway.
Yes.

I do not mean that part of
the railway which is not built yet, or the part that has gone into decay, but the part that is operative. I want to announce to the House that the Hudson Bay milway, so far as half of its mileage is concerned, is in operation. I think the minister himself can bear testimony that it is a good piece of railroad, and ought to be put to the utmost possible use. The minister's testimony does not stand alone. For two or three years we have been trying to persuade the House that this country through which the Hudson Bay line runs is as good a country as you can find in the west of Canada.
This does not depend upon recent visitors to that country. We have evidence dating as far back as that district has been known. Every government expedition sent in there has reported equally favourably about that country. Before the Senate committee, five years ago, J. B. Tyrell, a well-known government explorer, described that country through which the line ran for about 200 miles as being beautiful clay land, as good as any in Manitoba. We have other evidence which all goes to back up what the minister has said. I will detain the House just for a moment in reading the evidence of Mr. Mc-Innes, a member of the Geological survey, who went in there some years ago:
In summing up his impressions of what he designates "the gently rolling clay covered country", Mr. Wm. Mclnnes, of the Geological survey, wrote:
"Of the whole of this extensive plateauland, extending from the valley of the Nelson river westward to near Burntwood and Wekusko lakes (west long. 99 degrees, 46 min.), northerly at least to beyond latitude 56 d., and southerly to the limestone escarpment, an area of about 10,000 sq. miles, it may be said it is characterized by a heavy clay soil entirely free from boulders. Lacustrine clays, composed of the rock flour once held in suspension by glacial streams and deposited by them as they reached the quiet waters of a great lake, are essentially the soils of this region; there is no distinct surface soil clearly separable from the clay subsoil, the one merges gradually into the other, the clayey character of the soil being strongly apparent at the very surface where merely the shallow cover of decaying leaves and other vegetation is scraped away. Generally for from five inches to over a foot down the clay is deep brown in colour from the admixture of vegetable matter, and quite friable, and the rootlets of even the smaller surface vegetation reach down far below this level, though on the tops of many of the ridges the light buff-coloured clay, without any appreciable colouration from vegetable matter, comes to the surface. The rolling character of the plateau generally provides fair drainage, but over considerable areas in its central portion, far from the valleys of the larger streams, there are large tracts that have not sufficient gradients for the proper flow of the surface water but could be made available for agricultural uses by being artificially drained."
And further, this is his description of the climate:
Mr. Mclnnes gave particular attention to the question of climate, which he rightly considered of "vital importance in connection with this region". He kept a careful record of temperatures, and from the time it was "begun on the 19th of June until the night of the 29th September, when the thermometer fell to 26 d., there was no frost that affected even tender vegetation. On the night of the 10th of August the temperature fell to the freezing point, but did not get low enough to do damage at least in the valley of Grassy river, though some of the potato vines on the summit of the high ridge north of the Pas were slightly touched". He was convinced that the "district is not at all too cold for general agricultural operations. The longer daily duration of sunlight in these high latitudes must be taken into consideration and for purposes of comparison with more southerly localities yearly averages of temperature are of no value."
Through this agricultural region described by Mr. Mclnnes, the Hudson Bay road runs at the present time and is operating the whole of the distance through this clay belt. It seems to me to be a reasonable request that the government should, in a modest way, without going to a great deal of expense, institute

some form of experimental station to prove up this country. Already there is an abundance of proof, as the minister's own experience has confirmed, in regard'to the character of this land. Not only has the Minister of Agriculture for the Dominion been over that country, but so has the Minister of Agriculture for our province. As late as last summer, Mr. Bracken, in company with the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) took the same trip and covered the same ground as the Minister of Agriculture, and their impressions were almost identical with those of the Minister of Agriculture. We are always glad when visitors take that trip. We never try to keep any one away from viewing that country because our faith in it is very well established. It is a beautiful country to look at and I believe it is a good country. It may not be feasible to develop it immediately; but if we are going to operate these 214 miles of railway right through the middle of it, it is only reasonable to spend a little money in trying to determine its agricultural qualities. In this country, even in Manitoba, we have a class of farmer who likes to mix his agricultural operations with a little fishing or other occupations of that kind. I think we have many of them who are trying to eke out a living on land that is not equal in any respect to the land I have described. I think there are, in Europe, especially in northern Europe, farmers who would be only too glad of the opportunity this district gives. It may not be possible to open up the land extensively to settlers of any kind for some time, but in view of the ultimate completion of the Hudson Bay line and the fact that 214 miles of it are being operated every week, it is only reasonable that the government should follow up the personal investigations of the Minister of Agriculture and try out, in a scientific way, what the soil and climate of this immense northern clay belt of 10,000 square miles can really do. I hope the minister has given some attention to that and has already determined in some way or another to test out this country.

Has my hon. friend in mind any particular place along that road where he thinks we could get the best information in regard to the region? When I came back from there I met some of my experimental farm staff at Winnipeg at the rust conference, and I discussed with them the advisability of establishing either one of these small forty-acre illustration stations or possibly what we call a substation that will cost about $3,000 a year, either at mile 137, where there is a Store owned by a man named Atkinson 
or at mile 185, Where the apiple tree was growing to which I referred. I do not know which might be the better place and perhaps my hon. friend might give some suggestion.

I think either point would
be suitable, but probably the more northerly point would be desirable. It seems to be a suitable spot in many ways and, being more northerly than the other, it might give the region a better test.

When we reached Port Nelson we were surprised1 at many of the things we found there, but perhaps the most surprising thing to us was the fact that they had been ploughing. They had a splendid team of Percheron horses there and they had ploughed, I would say in the neighbourhood of three-quarters of an acre of land. The soil was rough on the surface, but we had a technical agriculturist with us and he was very much impressed with its possibilities. There are six men there under the superintendence of an engineer, Mr. Hazelwood, and I was wondering, in view of the fact that they had been attempting to cultivate some land there, if it would not be possible to have even there, without much expense, a kind of little illustration farm. That is to say, why not send up some seed to the engineer and the men in charge there, just as it is sent out to a little illustration station in my country and have them do a little experimenting on the side? The question may be asked as to its value. Well, one cannot help being impressed, in visiting the United States, by the erroneous opinions widespread there with regard to the southerly region of the provinces of Manitoba and1 Saskatchewan. Now if it could be shown that wild grasses or coarse grains can be grown at Port Nelson, I think it would prove of tremendous advertising value to our immigration authorities and would dispel a great many of the erroneous opinions that prevail to-day concerning that whole north country. do that. I did not know there was any experimental work carried on there. I think we could have some experiments made at a very small cost, especially now that the land

Consequently an altogether different set of problems have to be studied. I may say that I put in some time last summer in going into the business aspect of that farm, because I had felt that this was a vote which might well be reduced without impairing the efficiency of the farm. That is right.

At times we in that
country are deluged with literature and pestered by salesmen advocating some new kind of seed that is frost proof, rust proof, cutworm proof, drouth proof and everything else; in a word, the seed will make our fortunes. Hundreds of farmers have paid out good money on the strength of such representations. This experimental farm carries on experiments with grain seed offered for sale, and they advise the people of the district whether the seed is of the quality represented'. I made an estimate, based on the number of inquiries received by them and on the answers given me by farmers in the district, and I have reached the conclusion that the experimental work resulted in a saving of at least $80,000 because the farmers had not bought this useless seed that they would otherwise have wasted their money on. That negative result is something I had not considered before.
While I believe the farm has been carried on well, and while I believe that Mr. Reed and his staff are not only capable but enthusiastic, anxious to do their work and give all the service possible yet I think some lines of experimentation are being duplicated in the province. For instance, we have stock feeding experiments conducted at Edmonton, one hundred miles away, by the university under provincial auspices. We could very well come to an arrangement by which the federal farms and the provincial institutions might carry on experimental work along different lines and so avoid unnecessary duplication. Undoubtedly a considerable saving could be effected by a careful system along that line. After going through the district and observing the beneficial influence that has been exerted by the farm in the last year, for instance all through that part of the country the people are growing shelter belts, flowers, small fruits and shrubbery, I believe the farm has been worth while and is still doing exceedingly good work. But I should like to have the minister take steps so that as far as possible- and I discussed this very frankly with Mr. Reed-no duplication of research and experimental work should be continued as between the federal experimental farms and the provincial institutions. I believe it would be easy to arrange for certain phases of the work to be taken over absolutely by each class of institution, that is, when they are close together and1 the conditions are comparable. I have not made a careful estimate of the saving that could be effected, but when we discussed it we were agreed that undoubtedly a considerable saving would result and the money so saved might be devoted to the carrying on of experimental work that is now being neglected.

That is easily seen from the fact that farms in close proximity to experimental

farms are usually not much more up to date or better operated than ones at a distance from them. The reason for this is plain. The only farmers who can benefit are those who are willing to apply the result of the experiments to their own operations, and that can be done just as easily from the reports sent out from the farm by the man who lives twenty, thirty or forty miles away as by the man who is quite close to the farm itself. The work of experimenting, it seems to me, could be very well carried on in one central farm in a province. I cannot see the necessity of having three or four or more experimental farms in a province except under very exceptional circumstances. I have many times heard the criticism that there is too much overlapping and that there are too many experimental farms to be in the best interest of the work. Whether this is so or not, I am more than ever convinced to-night that it is by the statements of the minister himself. The minister told us some time ago that he really believed there were too many and that some might very well be done away with. If this is true, there never was a time when that policy was needed more than it is at present. Everywhere we are asked to practise economy. The government is faced with a falling revenue and there is a necessity for economy in expenditure. I think I can speak for the farming population in this country in saying that they are willing to bear their share of real economy in order to help balance revenue and expenditure. If what the minister has told us to-night is true that some farms could well be done away with, why not begin that policy now? Why the necessity of increasing the vote at this particular time when we should be trying to economize? What is the necessity of appointing a commission? The minister states that he believes there are too many of these farms. I cannot see why it is necessary in a matter of this kind when everything is within the knowledge of the minister and when he has the power, that he should appoint a commission to deal with a little matter like this. Especially when Mr. Preston is otherwise employed just now, why cannot the minister deal with it himself?
I have suggested that it might be possible to do with less experimental work; that in each province one or at the most two properly located and well conducted experimental farms should be sufficient. Other work necessary could be done in a small way possibly by illustration farms in different localities: If this is true-and I believe it is-I should like to ask the minister how many illustration farms
he has at the present time, where they are located by province, what is the approximate cost of operation and what is the average acreage?

The acreage is
about forty acres to the farm. Sometimes it is not quite that. There are 143 illustration farms. I have not given them by provinces, but while we are looking them up, I will tell my hon. friend why I think it is not advisable just now to make any reduction, until the provinces are consulted. I have discussed the question of reducing the number of provincial farms with two provincial authorities, Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan, and we have further deliberations to enter into before we can take any action, because it is not wise to take action with respect to this matter without consulting the respective provincial departments of agriculture and the respective governments. I have suggested, not a commission but a committee of disinterested men to look into the matter because their recommendations would be freer from, shall I say, bias, than would the recommendations of the minister. He might be accused of partiality towards his own province, his own party or his particular riding, and for that reason it would be better to have an independent committee. I could make the selection right now, for I have my mind almost made up as to where we might do the paring. But I question the advisability of doing it arbitrarily in that way. I think we should consult all the provincial governments affected before doing anything. It has been recommended that we should have co-operation with a view to cutting out the overlapping, and that is a good suggestion. One of the very first things to consider would be cooperation with the provinces in the matter of suggested changes; and in the meantime, while that is being decided, we should keep the farms in a respectable condition.

The minister has been
thinking of this matter for the past two or three years and he admits that it is nothing new. Why not begin in a small1 way and, instead of increasing the estimate $40,000, come forward with the former estimate if not a lower? Where are the 143 illustration farms located?
There are in British Columbia 13, in Alberta 15, in Saskatchewan 24, in Manitoba 8, in Ontario 8, in Quebec 43, in New Brunswick 20, in Nova Scotia 12 and in Prince Edward Island 8.

Has the minister any
record of the number of hogs the packers take
Supply-Agriculture

in in the course of a year on which a premium is paid?

Yes, we have a
record. The first year it was very small; it depends on the province. We get more in the Maritime provinces as a rule, in proportion to population, than anywhere else.
I think the highest number is in Ontario.

That is right, yes. Ontario and then the Maritime provinces. In some of the provinces the tendency has been to grow fat hogs, but in all of them there has been a marked improvement in the increased number of selects. This is a business that can be developed rapidly, and it is showing considerable improvement.

With regard to hog grading, the minister informed us a little while ago that the government graders were doing good work. But he admits that a great many of those hogs shipped direct to the stockyards are not graded at all.
Those shipped to the stockyards are graded1 there; the drovers do not grade them.

The producer does
not get the benefit. Why are hogs not bought according to quality the same as beef animals? Why employ an army of graders to grade hogs for the packing companies, who should buy their hogs according to quality as they do beef animals? The minister knows very well that while he employs graders to go to the packing companies he keeps no check on the meat that passes through the packing houses. He can give no information concerning the proportion of the meat that is sold as select, but as a matter of fact it is all sold as select; they do not mark it anything else. The people of this country have to pay the price of select but they are not getting it. Why does the minister not exercise control over the packers as well as over the fanners? I do not see why we should have all these vexatious regulations governing the producer, while we give other people a free hand to do as they see fit. The minister has his officials all over Ontario just now threatening the people that unless they do so and1 so the law will be enforced. Egg grading, for instance, has to be carried out throughout the country; with what result? Eggs are sold as seconds just as the farmer sells his hogs, not as selects but for a lower grade, where they are not taken to the packing company. And this thing will result in a lower price paid for the eggs although a higher price 
will be charged the consumer. If there is one commodity in regard to which there is no necessity for all this process of grading by government officials it is eggs. Eggs are either good or bad; and as to size, you might sell them by weight if you cared to. At all events, I do not see why we should have an army of officials who do not encourage but rather discourage people who would like to do something. The whole fact is that we have too many restrictions. Here are two items in connection with which we are asked to vote upwards of $2,000,000. and the minister admits that a great deal of what is being done is practically useless.
I do not admit that.

Well, then, what
about the farms which the minister admits should be eliminated? Is that not an admission that they are useless? With regard to the graders, the minister knows very well that if there is anything that requires attention on the part of the officials of his department it is the food sold to the consumer. But nothing is done in that direction.

But that would only
take more inspectors.

Would it not be better to put the inspectors where they would do valuable work? The packing companies are anxious to have the graders do for them what they should have done for themselves years ago. There is no reason why they should not pay for the hogs they get on the basis of quality, just as they pay for beef animals. Why does the minister not employ graders to grade beef animals as well as hogs?

You have to start somewhere, and the proposition was worked out by the various provincial ministers, as well as the Swine Breeders' Association and the federal Department of Agriculture in the fall of 1921 before I came to Ottawa, as my hon. friend (Mr. Tolmie) knows. We took over the plant and we are doing our best to give it a chance; and I believe it will go, if we have not too many people in the country roaring against it. My hon. friend asks why we do not follow it up with grading bacon. Well, it takes all our time to get the graders to grade the hogs. We have had one of the best experts we could secure engaged in studying the question of bacon requirements, and he has gone to the Old Country in this connection. This gentleman came back and we discussed the subject with him on his return. The Dominion government was asked by Great Britain to appoint two representatives

Supply-Agriculture
on the Imperial Marketing committee, and this man we recommended as one. He is over there now and will complete his investigation in due course. But if we employ more graders, the first complaint will be registered by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) that we are stacking up another bunch of inspectors. You cannot have it both ways, Mr. Chairman. If new duties are to be imposed upon my department I must have additional men. We are going along in the direction my hon. friend indicates as rapidly as we can get the men and the money.

Is the committee
to infer from the minister's remarks that he proposes to appoint graders to grade beef animals too?

No. There is no
demand for that.

There certainly has
not been a demand for the egg graders. I can assure the minister that there are very pronounced protests against these obnoxious restrictions.	#

For anybody who
wants to make political capital out of it. There is a complete system of egg grading in Prince Edward Island and the other Maritime provinces, also in the three prairie provinces. The only place where we have had to do any stimulating to get the system adopted is in the province my hon. friend comes from, and I d'o not know whether his agitation has retarded its adoption or not.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, this is the province wherei the people have to work for a living. The minister informed us how the westerner could produce beef cattle successfully by going around the hotels in white pants and starched collars. We cannot produce beef in Ontario that way.
I did not recommend that system anywhere.

That may be the
case in western Canada; in Ontario the minister may impose all the restrictions he likes, but he cannot force the people to produce this stuff if they do not wish to do so.

I am not trying
to.
I am trying to improve them.
I should like to know the cost of these Seasonal Hints.
My hon. friend spoke about publications.

Yes, the publications I referred to are the reports of the experimental farms, which reports are not available to the prospective immigrant. The shipping agents in the Old Country naturally get all the information they can about Canada, but this information so far as Ontario is concerned is practically a blank; they see abundance of
Supply-A griculture

it with regard to farms located in. all the [DOT]other provinces. This is the penalty Ontario pays for having borne the cost of this experimental work herself. The same discrimination against Ontario prevails in the Immigration department. The provincial government for years has had to do this work and pay for it, while the federal government has been doing it for all the other provinces. This is absolutely unfair. The minister exclaims, " Why, if these things are not done for the other provinces they will likely do them themselves." But why penalize them for bearing the expense? Why should Ontario suffer by reason of the fact that the federal government does little or nothing for experimental work in the province, and fails to furnish the prospective immigrant with the information he is seeking about farming opportunities in Ontario. These Seasonal Hints which are sent all over Ontario are really an insult to the people. What do they cost?
About $5,000.

A little earlier this evening the minister remarked that Essex and Kent were great tobacco-producing counties. )I would ask him not to forget to add the county of Elgin the next time he is talking about tobacco production in Ontario. During the past few years the county of Elgin has had from 700 to 1,000 acres under tobacco, and we expect this coming season the area will ibe increased to about 1,500 acres. The county produces very good tobacco. With respect to the regulations governing the premium on bacon hogs, is it not about time the minister made a change so that the producer may receive the benefit?

We changed them a few months ago. Only two grades are graded by the graders now, " thick-smooth " and "select." As to the other grades, the buyer land the seller do their own negotiating, and if they disagree as to the grade they call in the grader to arbitrate.
The local shipper you are referring to now?

There is no way of reaching the local shipper. He Is in the same position as the local shipper of grain. The man who sells to a local shipper on a flat rate basis cannot get the benefit of any grade. The system cannot be applied to the man who will not use his Chances of co-operating with his neighbours and shipping in car lots.
The minister informed the committee a few moments ago that we have 143 illustration stations. Are those stations owned by the government or is the land rented?
The farms are owned by the farmers and operated by them under the advice and supervision of a member of the experimental farm staff.

What is the average
cost of these illustration farms?
About $300.

I have been studying this question of experimental farms and I have come to the conclusion that the work in that connection is not giving the benefit to the people that it should, simply because it is impossible to get to the farmers the information that can be derived from that work. I suggest that the illustration station is far more valuable than some of the present experimental farms and that it would well repay this country if we put more money into the illustration stations and less into the experimental farm work. I have had the pleasure on more than one occasion of observing the work of these illustration stations. They are usually very close to a small town or village, on highways that are much used by the farmers, and as the farmers go to market or to town, as the case may be, they pass these illustration stations and see what is being done. Personally I believe that the results would be more beneficial if the illustration station plan was extended and the experimental farm work reduced.
Thank you.

Most of the information I intended to ask for has been given in answer to the hon. member (Mr. Gardiner). Like him, I have been of the opinion that good results could be accomplished by increasing the work of the illustration farms, and that without greatly burdening the taxpayer. What I wanted to know was about the average cost. Am I correct in inferring that the average size is about fifty acres?
Forty.

A year or two ago the federal department entered into some kind of arrangement with regard to the importation of sheep, and I think that policy was carried out last year. Is it the intention to continue it?

I think last year was the first year we adopted that policy. A few Rambouillets have been brought in from the United States by the Sheep Breeders' As-

Supply-A griculture
sociation, with some assistance and supervision by members of the Department of Agriculture, who assisted in making the selections. All the other breeds we have been handling are prohibited entry under the embargo on account of the foot and mouth disease.

Two years ago the
minister intimated that the department intended to import pure bred animals and to use the central farms as distributing centres to supply the surrounding districts. Many complaints have been made as to the unfairness of the government's entering into competition with people engaged in legitimate business, yet the government have been paying officials to go over to the Old Land, buy stock there, bring it out here and sell it in competition with breeders of live stock in this country. Does he consider that that is a proper policy for the government to pursue?

We endeavour to
carry only such stock as the capacity of each farm will permit. We have practically no complaints of the character my hon. friend has mentioned; in fact, our activities develop such a demand throughout the country for pure bred stock and better stock that the result has been to increase rather than to lessen the sales to private breeders. The same question came up some years ago in connection with the distribution of trees by the Forestry department. It was urged that the private nurseries would be injured, but the reverse actually happened; the business of the nurseries was increased very considerably.

I have received a
letter from Nova Scotia to-day complaining about this very matter and pointing out the unfairness of the government's entering into this business in competition with those in this country who have invested their money in it and have been endeavouring to carry on. I do not think this is a matter that comes within the province of the federal government. The government have enough to do to look after things that are absolutely necessary, and they should not venture into such new fields as the Department of Agriculture have been entering upon. Many vexatious restrictions have been put into force by that department during the last few years, but I believe this establishing of breeding depots at these farms is about the worst. The minister says they are carrying on this work just to the capacity of the farms. Well, what is the capacity of the farms? If you import
stock and keep it there a week, two weeks or a month-
We do not do that at all.

The minister informed the House two years ago that that was what he proposed to do, and I believe a good deal of it has been done in the Maritime provinces as well as in other parts of the country. The minister intimated that was his policy.

My hon. friend has got the two problems mixed. These importations of sheep are made by the provinces, and we place them. We rarely import even breeding animals for the use of the farms, but occasionally we do import hogs and sheep. But we do not bring them here and then retail them to the farmers. We import only what we require for the various farms, and then we breed from them on our own farms. My hon. friend thinks we are doing a retail business in them, importing them and retailing them, but that is not the situation at all. We have not done that in one single instance.

I am afraid I shall
have to send for Hansard1 and read the minister's policy on this matter given a few years ago. I protested against it at the time, and I know complaints have kept on coming in. I received one to-day from Nova Scotia complaining of what the government were doing, and of the inferior class of animals that were being sold to them.

What is the minister
going to do with regard to assisting the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair? The city of Toronto has spent $2,000,000 on this fair, and it gets only a small grant towards the prize list from the government. The minister made a fine speech in Toronto, much better I think than he makes here, and promised the pioneers in that work some assistance. The city has spent $40,000,000 on the summer fair, very largely for the benefit of the agricultural industry, and then it comes along and spends $2,000,000 for the Royal Agricultural Fair for the development of the live stock industry of this country. An application has been made to the government for practical assistance, and I would like to know what the government is going to do. It is not a municipal matter at all, but a federal and provincial matter, because live stock is under the jurisdiction of both legislatures. The show is larger than the New York and Chicago shows. The minister himself said

Supply-A gricul ture
that 'it was the largest show on the continent when he spoke in Toronto at the opening of the fair. He has received a memorandum asking for assistance, and I would like to know what he is prepared to do. The association is composed practically of farmers; I do not think the city of Toronto has a single representative on the board, although the city has supplied all the money for the fair, which is far larger than Madison Square Garden. The city should not be left alone to carry the burden, because the fair is doing an educational work that is for the 'benefit of the live stock industry all over the country, and it is being done now at great cost to the taxpayers of the city of Toronto.

The annual grant to the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair, not of Toronto, but of Canada, is $25,000 a year, extending over ten years. They have requested additional! assistance, and that is under consideration. That is as far as I can go.

I notice an item in the Auditor General's report of $18,476 for free freight policy, which is included in this item we are discussing. There is another policy of car lot policy, for which there was an expenditure of $8,768. How does this apply? How is it that some provinces can avail themselves of this free freight policy and others not?

That policy was adopted in order to encourage the shipping of breeding animals back into the country. Take the case of one of our stock yards where there is a lot of breeding stock that should be kept on the farm. The farmer being hard up has shipped this stock into market; he may have been short of feed or of cash, or both. In order to encourage the return of that stock to the interior, which it should never have left, the government some six or eight years ago adopted this policy of assisting the farmer in buying this breeding stock at the respective stock yards and shipping it back to the interior. We have continued that policy up to this year. We have recently had a conference between the deputy minister and the live stock commissioner, and as a result, whether for good or evil, we are discontinuing the policy. A considerable amount of abuse has crept in under it. I am not criticizing the policy; I think it was all right when it was inaugurated, but certain abuses have crept in that render its discontinuance advisable.

This policy was to assist in shipping back young cattle from the 
west that had been sold on our eastern markets?
Yes.

Did it not apply to the shipping of feed cattle as well as breeding stock? The shipper from western Canada to Toronto could have these animals sent back at half carload rates, but in Ontario we have not any of these privileges. I am speaking of feeders for commercial purposes.

I think my hon.
friend refers to the first item, the free freight policy with respect to breeding stock. This other is with respect to steers. Assistance was given by the federal government for a number of years. We pay the transportation expenses of the purchaser and his hotel expenses, and the transportation companies knock off 25 per cent from the cost of transporting the animals. That was arranged with the railways just about the same time, some five or six years ago, and I understand that that is being eliminated also.

What I was particularly inquiring about was the policy of getting a half rate on cattle for feeding purposes. The western shipper into Ontario can get that rate, 'but the Ontario buyer cannot get it. Now is that fair?

I understand that
policy was extended to Ontario. I know the Ontario buyer got sufficient inducement to come out west to the feeder shows, in the way of cheaper freight rates and assistance all round both from the government and the railways, although I have not the
12	m. exact details, to encourage him to come out there and get animals for feeding purposes at a good figure and bring them back east. As far as the future is concerned, I understand that we are eliminating both that system and the free freight policy with respect to breeding stock.

I thought the minister was wrong, but if he is right I must be mistaken. The way he explained the matter was that if western cattle were shipped to Ontario there would be a reduction in the cost of transportation back to the west.
No.
That is what the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) stated.
No.

He talked about shipping
them back to the west.
