I think that was only to Winnipeg.
What goes to Winnipeg can be shipped to the prairies.
Yes, I did not think it extended any further than Winnipeg.

I must protest
against the impression which the minister's explanation leaves on members of the House. That does apply to Ontario. The shipper from the west can ship his stock to Ontario, he can sell it there and consign it out again at half rate. If it is consigned to a dealer in Toronto and sold there, and the purchaser purchases it in Toronto, he has to pay full car rates if he sends it outside. I know payment is evaded in many instances, but it is not honestly done, and should not be permitted, because many people send their cattle to Toronto, and in some instances, through the connivance of the commission men, can get the special rate. Why should this rate not apply to people all over the country?
The minister stated a few minutes ago that the purchaser's hotel fare was paid. Was that the Ontario purchaser who went to our city markets and purchased young western cattle?

In the local market. I do not know why they make a difference, but it only applies to stockyards, Winnipeg and the west; but an eastern man could go to the stockyards at Winnipeg and the west and get these, advantages and ship stuff down here. I do not know why it was not extended to the eastern stockyards at Toronto. I did not work out the policy, but it was in force when we started to administer this work, and certain abuses have crept in, with the result that we are dropping all these things.
The hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) left the inference from his remarks that the purchaser from Ontario did not benefit by this reduced fare.
He is wrong.

I have been on the market considerable myself, and I know it was the practice of Ontario buyers to go in and buy western stock or cattle and have them shipped out to their homes without any freight charge, but the Ontario purchaser did get the benefit of it.

I referred to a case where the westerner sold his cattle at Toronto market, as has been done in many instances, 53
but some of the dealers arranged to have those cattle shipped out, even though they were not consigned by the party who shipped them there at all. Another farmer comes in and buys a mixed load from two dealers, and does not get that advantage. It is an unfair thing and the regulations are being evaded. In many instances, people get that rate, but they do not get it honestly. If the western shipper consigns his stuff right through to the dealer and it is purchased direct on the market from that dealer, he gets the benefit. But if it is purchased with a mixed load he does not get any benefit a.t all.

I beg pardon. It was the practice for two or three falls that when western cattle consigned to commission men in Toronto market sold again as stocker cattle out through the country there was no freight charge from Toronto to the distributing point. It had to be western cattle. It did not matter whether you bought them out of half a dozen loads, as long as they were all western cattle. It was not necessary that they should all be purchased out of the one car

I think the hon. member is in error, and if we had a little more time I believe we would be able to convince our western friends that they have many privileges that we in the east do not have, even in regard to the Hudson Bay railway which the country will have to build for them. In the province of Ontario we have offered to build a line through to Hudson bay, and we are going to do it ourselves. I think the minister might move that the committee rise.
That is what the member has been playing for all night.

I do not think that remark is justified. The minister should be fair sometimes. He has done more talking than anybody else. The hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) has only been talking for the last half hour, and the minister has made long and probably excellent speeches.
I harm to, I cannot get out of it.

I am not complaining, but it is not fair for the minister to charge the hon. member with killing time and holding this vote back till twelve. He certainly has not. I do not know what the understanding as to adjournment is. I thought the idea was to sit till eleven, unless we were given some notification to the contrary. It

Supply-Agriculture

is after twelve o'clock now, and I have no doubt the minister will move the adjournment.

We would like to have the item passed. We have referred to the live stock this evening and reverted to a former vote, and discussed experimental farms until I think we have covered the ground better than we have ever done on any previous occasion. We have to judge our hon. friend from South Oxford by his conduct of former years. He may not have wanted to prevent the item going through to-night, but we know his attitude generally.

I do not want the minister to impute wrong motives. I think I have been reasonable in my request for information, and if the minister had been more frank with the committee it would have been better for the committee and for himself. He has certainly given information on two or three different questions on different occasions, and taken up a good deal of time in doing so, when he might very well have given a direct answer. He has informed the committee that there are a large number of these things they propose cutting out, even the last item to which I have referred in regard to' the assistance in freight rates. Why is the minister asking for as large an item as he asked for a year .ago in regard to live stock; and an increase of $40,000 in the item for experimental farms, when he admits that a great deal of pruning might be done and much money saved in that respect? Surely some information should be given in regard to that.

The work in other lines is increasing and requiring more money. We dropped off the work which had been developed to the point where its usefulness ceased or its purpose was accomplished, but other activities required more money.
What new activities are being undertaken in connection with this?
Experimental farms. I gave that information.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That information has already been given to the committee, and the minister does not require to give it again.
I object to any blocking of any reasonable information. I asked for information in regard to live stock and it has not been given.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The information asked for by the hon. member was given and the minister does not require to give it seriatim the second time. As it has already been
fSir Henry Drayton.]
given to the committee, to give it again would mean irrelevancy and the debate continuing over the same ground1 the second time.

I must insist that
to my knowledge the information for which I have asked has not been given, that is with regard to new activities in connection with the item under live stock.

The minister mentioned that it was the intention of the department to cease giving this assistance on freight to stock or cattle in Ontario. I differ slightly from the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) in saying that this assistance is given only to western farmers. It was taken advantageously by the .farmers of Ontario, and I think they appreciated it fully as much as the western people because it afforded them an opportunity to get good stock and receive some assistance in connection with it. I am satisfied1 that the Department of Agriculture is carrying on a good many side lines that might much more easily be cut out than such a direct aissistance to agriculture as this is, and I think it is something that should be continued.
Has my hon. friend reference more to the feeder shows that I think he is familiar with?
No.

I am sorry we have decided to cut it out for the reason I have given. Many abuses were creeping in and we found we could use the money to better advantage elsewhere. We will continue though, the encouragement for eastern men to go west to these stacker or feeder shows at Winnipeg, Moose Jaw or Calgary, because we find that they like our class of feeder animals there very well and they assist the sales very materially by their activities.

What is the nature of
the feeder shows the minister mentions?

I read them over
very fully. I want to answer the hon. member for South Oxford as to the new work we are taking over. This branch is taking over the cow testing for butter fat, not for tuberculosis. An additional amount is required for that. It was formerly conducted by the Dairy branch.

I did not hear the
minister's explanation, but I am not going to ask him to repeat it because it was my fault possibly for not being present. As regards the feeder shows, they may be doing a certain amount of good, but the department is assisting eastern people and there will be

Disablement Fund
only a very limited number of Ontario fanners who will be able to go to these shows. At the same time the western stocker cattle must come to Ontario to be finished for the export market, so as to be in the condition we should try to put them into before they leave the country. Therefore, I feel that the department will be doing more good in assisting the distribution of stocker cattle from the central markets into eastern Canada than by assisting a few individual farmers in going to those western shows.

There may be
something in that, but there were certain abuses that I do not care to mention.

The matter referred to by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Thurston) is very important in the older province. There is certainly not much advantage in shipping stockers to the Old Country when it costs just as much in ocean rates for a thin animal as for one that is finished. If these animals can be finished in this country, so much the better for the country. That is the point that should be encouraged. The hon. member for Victoria must have shipped the feeders to which he has been referring through the farmers co-operative.
Not all of them.

I know they have
been able by some means to ship those cattle out where others did not obtain the same rates which they did. I am not saying this in any way disparagingly of the practice, because I know of instances where stock has been shipped out by commission agents as these people really are. I know in many other instances they have not been able to avail themselves of this assistance. The department might very well encourage the giving of cheap rates on feeder cattle so as to have them sent back and finished on the farms. I do not know of any expenditure which could be made with better results.

Does the hon. member
think he is entitled to rates from the prairies to Ontario when we do not get them to British Columbia?

I am not speaking
about any particular province. I am speaking about a general practice over this Dominion, not confined to any province as it is to-day.
